title: Soon ashes
hook: soon you'll be ashes; meanwhile, revere and do good (Meditations 5.33)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bad breath: he has the mouth he has. Your line was it's his mouth.

Ashes is a word people tend to keep at a distance, for funerals and a few solemn days a year. Marcus Aurelius kept it closer. In book five, entry thirty-three, he writes it to himself very plainly: you'll be ashes soon. Then, in the same breath, he asks what a person should do with the time in between. His answer is short, and it isn't gloomy at all. It's a to-do list.
screen: `WE KEEP THE WORD AT A DISTANCE.` → `MARCUS KEPT IT CLOSE.` → `SOON ASHES.`

segments.voice: Soon, very soon, Marcus writes, you'll be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name. And a name is only a sound and an echo. Then he looks at what people spend their lives fighting over. The things most prized in life, he says, are empty and small: puppies snapping at each other, children quarreling, laughing, and then crying a minute later. He borrows a phrase from the Greek poet Hesiod, about virtues fleeing the wide earth for Olympus, and applies it to faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth. A wry picture of a world that often forgets what matters. So what holds him here, he asks, since the things we sense are always changing and our senses are easily fooled? His answer: wait calmly for the end, whatever it turns out to be. And meanwhile, what's enough? To revere the gods and speak well of them. To do good to people. To bear with them, and to hold back. And to remember that whatever lies outside your own small flesh and breath is not yours and not up to you. Marcus doesn't use ashes to stop himself living. He uses it to clear the desk. The squabbles drop off. What's left fits on a card: reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. For him, reverence meant the gods of Stoic belief; readers on many paths keep that part in their own words, or in none. The rest is open to anyone: do good, now, while there's a now.
screen: `SOON ASHES, AND A NAME, OR NOT EVEN.` · `PUPPIES SNAPPING, CHILDREN QUARRELING.` · `WHAT HOLDS YOU HERE?` · `MEANWHILE: REVERE, DO GOOD, BEAR.` · then, large: `MEANWHILE, DO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Say the word quietly to yourself, ashes, and let it be plain, not frightening. Then feel your breath, warm and still here. Meanwhile: bring to mind one small good act within reach, a message, a kindness, a bit of patience, and let that be enough.
Soon ashes. Marcus reminds himself he'll soon be ashes and a name; meanwhile, it's enough to revere, to do good, and to bear with people. Today's word.
Your line: meanwhile, do good. Reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. Day five hundred seventy-one, done.

notes: 5.33 paraphrased: soon, very soon, you will be ashes or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; a name is sound and echo; the things much valued in life are empty, rotten, trifling, like little dogs biting one another, little children quarreling, laughing, then crying; fidelity, modesty, justice and truth are fled 'Up to Olympus from the wide-spread earth' (Hesiod); what then detains you here? wait in tranquility for the end, whether extinction or removal elsewhere; until then, what is sufficient? to venerate the gods and bless them, to do good to men, to practice tolerance and self-restraint; and to remember that what is beyond the limits of the poor flesh and breath is neither yours nor in your power. Hesiod, Works and Days c. 197–201 (Aidos and Nemesis leaving the earth); Marcus's list of four virtues may be his adaptation. Confirm line reference and wording of the paraphrase.
